utterances.text: And if you were to believe what the accused were saying in your presence, would it then be correct if I were to say that it would be the responsibility of the public prosecutor to take certain actions, measures, with regards to the reasonable grounds that were stated in your presence?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't know what you precisely are referring to. Could you clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If, for instance, maybe this did not happen in your presence, but let's assume that it had happened, that some of the accused had serious injuries, and complained of sustaining them through the ill-treatment by the police, would it then be correct that it would be your responsibility, of you, the public prosecutor, to take actions to investigate whether those claims were justified, those claims made by the accused?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: First, it is the obligation of the investigating judge to enter in the record all the visible injuries. If there are visible injuries, then upon the completion of the interview, the accused is sent to a physician, where an expert, a doctor, would identify the type of the injury. After that, if these are more serious injuries, then it is the -- the obligation of the prosecutor to further investigate how these injuries have been inflicted. Usually, there is a forensic expertise to identify how these injuries have been inflicted, what have they been inflicted with, so then the procedure, the legal procedure is the same as for any other type of criminal act.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if the court record contained a suspicion that a police officer did something illegal, then, as you have just stated, the investigating judge would the duty to verify the defence presented by the accused and also obtain other evidence, medical evidence or other statements of witnesses; and after that, the public prosecutor would act within the competences. And so I'm asking again: The police could not know what has been stated and what has been made part of the criminal record in the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: In the criminal files of the court, the judge has access to them, the prosecutor has access to them, the accused, and his counsel. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if would just happen that in the given circumstances the court failed to take all the actions that were its duty, as you have stated, or the prosecutor failed to do the follow-up actions, the police could have no influence over that, in no way. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: No. That would be a failing to act by the investigating judge and the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, we discussed a while ago the situation where the prosecutor -- actually, the investigating judge could ask the police to render assistance also in the course of the actual investigation. I would like to ask you now to look at the document under the tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Exhibit P47. Macedonian page 92, while the English page ET-0463-8982-01. That is the supplementary opinion of the criminalistics, criminal techniques, as it is stated in the document, of the Ministry of Interior. And the next document under tab 25, that is Exhibit P47. Macedonian page 90, while the English page is ET-0463-8980-01. So this is, again, a supplementary opinion that is submitted upon a court request.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to these exhibits, I would like to ask you, Ms. Ruskovska, is it correct that the paraffin glove, as evidence of presence of nitrate particles on a body of a given person, was used often in relation to crimes involving use of fire-arms.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this last document, there is the signature of the engineer, Sylvija Kunovska, as an expert witness. Do you know Ms. Kunovska?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, as a prosecutor acting within a case, you are making your best efforts to get the best opinions from the experts available in the Republic of Macedonia, in relation to a case that are you in charge with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the same is done by the investigating judge in the court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Basically, the investigating judge does it because the expertise needs to be taken. The court has the budget to pay for them, so all the expertise are conducted through the court or upon our request. Upon the request of the prosecutor's office, these are ordered by the investigating judge for any expertise, for post-mortem, for traffic expertise, for like powder particles expertise, anything. Everything goes through the investigating judge when the case is in the investigating stage. If it is in the stage of a trial, then that is requested by the president of the court chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in this case, against some persons from Ljuboten, you had also the expertise, expert report that showed the presence of nitrate particles. That was one of the exhibits accompanying the indictment, presence of particles in persons who were detained. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document we have in front of us shows that the judge requested an additional opinion from the expert who was in charge. So could you tell me, please, whether you, in your practice or in this specific case, requested that the expert, apart from the description of the finding, the presence of nitrate particles, gives an opinion of what would be the reason of where would those particles found on the hands of the accused originate from?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your practice, were you ever confronted with an opinion that was based also on the overall circumstances that the court or the expert took into consideration to then give their opinion?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Are you referring to the nitrate particles?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. I had a recent case like that; whereby, the expert stated that the nitrate particles could originate from various sources, not only from gun powder. But according to their opinion, they are stratification. The position of -- the position of certain parts of the hands can indicate with high probability that they can originate from gun powder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It appears to the Prosecution that through this witness we are now receiving expert opinion from another witness in some other case apparently in Macedonia, and it seems to me that this is of little assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wish to show to the Court what is the practice followed by all bodies, especially the law enforcement bodies in the Republic of Macedonia, because they don't have any other possibilities. So if you allow me, I have just one more question in relation to this witness [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Ms. Ruskovska, tell me, please, whether what you requested in the case against the -- versus the people from Ljuboten, in relation to the nitrate particles expert report, was the best you could get in the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not have any other institution. You had no funds to verify whether these expert report was absolutely accurate anywhere else in the world; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you relied, among other things, also on the expert reports submit to the you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: That's what there are experts for, to be able to rely on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Maybe it is incorrectly entered in the transcript. I said that in relation to this paraffin glove test, I have only this these questions I have asked; while in the line 18, it is written that I have just few more questions, which would be incorrect. I have a number of questions still pending, but I will, anyhow, complete my cross-examination soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, were you -- in the course of this procedure, did you know that a person that an investigation was needed for, that that person had died in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to say that at that time case, your colleague, Serafimovski acted, could you recall that that was his case?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I couldn't. There were too many people there, so I don't know which person was part of which case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you can't recall who of your colleagues exactly had the named case, I would only ask you: You surely know your colleague, Jovan Serafimovski, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We used to work together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a part of the statement that your colleague, Jovan Serafimovski, gave on 19th of December, 2005 to the ICTY investigators, and I would like to ask you a few questions in relation to that. In point 10 of that statement of the 19th of December 2007, Jovan Serafimovski has stated: "In respect to the Atulla Qaili case mentioned in part 7 of the request, on 14th of August, 2001, I didn't know that he is already dead. About the death of Atulla Qaili, I learned when I received the written information from the investigating judge, Velce Pancevski. "My duty was to identify the cause of death of Atulla Qaili. We heard that he has been hurt during the conflict with the Macedonian security forces in the village of Ljuboten. I learned from the press that the police was there. I do not know what unit was there. I did not know the unit, nor the names of the police or the army officials that were involved in the death of Atulla Qaili. I did not try to investigate who was related to the death of Atulla Qaili." In respect to this, and since you have said earlier that some significant injuries should be further investigated by the investigating judge, that is, the competent prosecutor, do you think that your colleague, Jovan Serafimovski, rightly said that it was his duty at that moment to investigate information he received from the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: In my opinion, first, in agreement with the investigating judge, the post-mortem protocol was ordered. After such post-mortem protocol was prepared, and depending on the injuries causing the death and the indications that this presents, then we were supposed to investigate it; we, the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then the post-mortem protocol is only sent to the investigating judge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police does not receive such a post-mortem report.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also spoke about the very difficult conditions under which you used to work; you and the court. Tell me, please, did any of the suspects, that you -- to which interviews you participated, mention any person against which it would be possible to initiate then a procedure?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that in some conflicts where large numbers of persons are involved, it is very difficult, both for the police and for the prosecutor and for the court, to establish a particular perpetrator, unless the persons participating in the conflict name the person?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, always when they're involved, more persons is difficult to identify who -- who has done what precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in your statement, but I'll ask you again: Is it correct that you, your colleagues, the judges, all did your very best in compliance with the law, regardless of the complicated conditions that obtained at the time for the work of the judges and the prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: We really tried to do our best, most professionally. So if we have made a mistake, that wasn't on purpose; but in all this pressure, in all that pressure ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we have already said that when there is unknown perpetrator, only certain investigative actions can be undertaken, but not an investigation, not a full-blown investigation. And we have already seen official records and notes written by judges and prosecutors, showing that they were unable to enter the village of Ljuboten to establish facts concerning the death of those persons. The only thing that possibly be done was to exhume the bodies that had been buried?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this could only be ordered by the investigating judge at the proposal of the prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The police, or the Ministry of Interior, was unable to carry out this investigative activity or to establish whether those persons had been killed and why.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure itself stipulates that upon the proposal of the public prosecutor, the investigating judge orders exhumation. So in accordance to the law, the obligation of any other body is not prescribed to carry out that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the document in tab 35.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Exhibit P55. Macedonian page 3; English page P002-1148-1. This is the proposal submitted by the basic public prosecutor's office on the 10th of September, 2001 for the undertaking of certain investigation actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 of this proposal, it says that, "The public prosecutor's office, in relation to this case, acting pursuant to Article 148, paragraph 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, and upon the written initiative of the Minister of the Interior, which has been handed to the above-named during duty hours, during outside the regular working hours, on the 7th of September, 2001, gives a proposal on undertaking certain investigation actions." Is it correct that this is a lawful proposal submitted by the competent prosecutor following an initiative from the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it looks like from the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at document -- the document in tab 36, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D177. Macedonian page 1D-1941. And we can look at all three pages, 1942, and 1943. English page 1D-1944, 1D-1945, and 1D-1946. Your Honours, I wish only to mention that this document is Exhibit D49 -- INTERPRETER: Interpreter's correction: P49.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as there was no translation, we added the translation so that Your Honours might have the complete document in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at tab 37 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's Exhibit P55. Macedonian page 4; English page ET-N002-1149-1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the document you have in your binder. The document emanates from the Ministry of Interior, the public security directorate. The document is dated the 7th of August, 2001. But in the previous document, you saw that the Ministry of Interior provided information about a mistake in the date and submitted the first page with a correct date, which was the 7th of September, 2001. As we have just seen that it was your colleague, Mr. Sakic, who dealt with this case, is this the proposal sent by the ministry to the public prosecutor and the investigating judge to be sure it is a proposal, but your colleague properly treated it as an initiative to continue with investigative actions in order to determine what exactly happened in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, Ms. Ruskovska, that practically this kind of initiative, coming from the Ministry of Interior, shows that the ministry did more than it was duty-bound under the law to do, because it is encouraged the proper organs to continue with their investigation into the events at Ljuboten. Would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please look at tab 38 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our 65 ter exhibit, 1D-178. Macedonian page 1D-1947; English 1D-1948. Your Honours, this document, again, is part of P49, but there is no translation, so we have a draft translation for the purposes of today's testimony, and we shall submit the official translation when we receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, this Official Note was signed by investigating judge, Dragan Nikoloveski. You now Judge Nikoloveski, do you not?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at this document, you can see that the investigating judge immediately agreed to the proposal submitted on the 10th of September by the public prosecutor's office, and a meeting was held in the Institute for Forensic Medicine, attended, apart from the judge and the prosecutor, by representatives of the Ministry of Interior, from the security sector in Skopje; and at this meeting, further measures were discussed in order to continue the investigation into the events at Ljuboten. Does this show, Ms. Ruskovska, that the investigation into the events at Ljuboten did not stop, but that both the Ministry of Interior and the prosecutor and the judge opened up further investigations against unknown perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, it surely has been open, because you can see the number of the file at the top, as far as I was able to notice. The file number E-601/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please now look at tab 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is our 65 ter 1D-179. Macedonian page 1D-1949 and the English 1D-50. Your Honours, this is also part of P49. There was no translation, so we have provided the draft translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, you see, again, before you a letter concerning investigation in the Ljuboten event, and it is a request by the investigating judge to the director of the public safety bureau, Goran Mitevski, asking that the police obtain the additional information needed, so that the judge can enter the village and carry out the exhumation and post-mortems as proposed. Does this also show, Ms. Ruskovska, that the various organs attempted to carry out a thorough investigation into the events in Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. This bears the same number that the case was initiated indicated with, about the exhumation, about the special investigating measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, are you aware that, in 2001, the Albanian population did not wish to cooperate with the state organs of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I know that part of the Albanian population in the crisis areas was not willing to cooperate. I can only speak about that part of the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do the prosecutor's office ant the court still meet with obstruction by Albanian groups in the crisis-affected areas?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that Albanians, including Albanians from the village of Ljuboten, did not want to report deaths, and this caused great problems when death certificates had to be issued?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can't remember now. If you're talking about that period in 2001, I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Would you please look at document in tab 40?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic we've now gone over time for this session. We have given you very free hand, but tried to encourage you to be mindful of time. It's now been a very long time that have you been questioning. Can you indicate where you are with your time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have about ten minutes of questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, please take a look at tab 40 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P104. It's one page; one in English and one in Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you see from the title, this is a document by the Cair Department for Internal Affairs. Look at the Official Note, please. You said just a while ago that it was very difficult in the crisis-affected areas to talk to members of the Albanian population. In this Official Note, it's evident that the official organ of the Ministry of Internal Affairs tried to talk about Kenan Salievski, the president of the Crisis Staff, and it says: "On the 16th of November, 2001, Kenan Salievski called at the Department for Internal Affairs in Cair; and he said that after having consulted the village board from the village of Ljuboten, he couldn't give us any information either about the event or about the deceased persons." Does this document confirm what you know from the time about the unwillingness of the Albanian population in certain areas to cooperate with official state organs of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a problem in the transcript, but I see it's been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did these problems also cause the failure to detect the perpetrators of other crimes and bring them before the court?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: What other crimes are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any such experiences; for example, the persons who placed explosives in Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: The perpetrators were not discovered and no procedure was instigated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After completing the investigation, you and your colleagues felt there was sufficient grounds to raise an indictment, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: When it's investigation was completed, the case was presented before the collegium of the senior public prosecutor's office in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your indictments were confirmed by the court, were they not?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: The senior public prosecutor's office made the decision, stating that sufficient evidence was present to then raise an indictment. So this was not a decision by me and the two other colleagues processing the case only. This was a decision behind which the entire senior public prosecutor's office in Skopje stood; and after the indictment was filed, then the verdict became also final.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But no trial was ever held, so the evidence collected during the investigation could not be tested in court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No trial was held because of the efforts to carry out the framework agreement or the persons were granted amnesty [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the same time, in late 2001, the Law on Amnesty was being prepared; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 62, line 10, it says "the persons were granted amnesty." I said "that by a decree of the president of the country, the persons were granted amnesty." Pardoned. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that preparations were in progress and finally the Law on Amnesty was adopted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to look now under tab 42 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the Exhibit P83. Macedonian page is N000-9977, and the English page is N000-9207.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You recognise here the wording of the Law on Amnesty, is that correct, under tab 42 -- behind tab 42?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: No, because you said five laws. You said five laws. That's why I got confused. We only have one law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Maybe I made a mistake. The Law on Amnesty was adopted. And on this page, you recognise the decree pronouncing the Law on Amnesty and the Article 1 of that law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2, it is stated the amnesty also applies to persons" -- I apologise. In paragraph 1, it is set forth who are the persons benefiting from amnesty; and at the end of this paragraph, it is stated that those are the persons on whom there is a reasonable doubt that they had prepared or committed crimes related to the conflict in 2001, ending with the 26th of September, 2002. So my question is: Is it correct, Ms. Ruskovska, that this law applied to all persons who had allegedly committed crimes related to the conflict up until the 26th of September?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it also applies to both Albanians and Macedonians and members of other communities without any discrimination; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now a question. I'm not sure whether you will be able to answer it, but I will still ask it. If by any chance you had information that some person, member of the police or the army forces, ill-treated a Ljuboten villager, would you consider that these persons are included in the amnesty provided by this law?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: As a prosecutor, I usually dwell on theoretical questions, and it is very give difficult to provide an answer to this. It is dependent on the case. But most probably, I can't speak with certainty, but most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this would mainly be because, at you explained earlier, you treated these events under the domestic law, as general crimes, severe breaches, or less severe breaches under the domestic law, and you did not think that the conduct of the police or the army would be the subject of the international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, in relation to the law. This law excluded responsibility only for the offences that were the -- on which the International Criminal Tribunal has started procedures. In 2001 and in 2002, you had no information that there was a procedure before the International Criminal Tribunal against any person from Macedonia, member of the police or the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I personally had know information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at the end, just two or three more questions. You answered many of my questions related to the actions and the competences of your colleagues, prosecutors, as well as the judges. Can I say that all these persons, both prosecutors and judges, were professionals with significant experience in the criminal procedures in the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: What persons are you referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We've mentioned your colleagues: Sakic, Serafimovski, Judge Ognen Stavrev, Judge Niklovski, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is all relative. Some of them had more experience; some of them had less experience. So, for example, Sakic has been a prosecutor for 20 years before that. We were for five years, but all of us had experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And all of you made the best of efforts to work in accordance with the law and to respect all the rights of the accused in the procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not make any difference, any discrimination whether the accused were Macedonians or Albanians.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I can say that we have not done that in the past and we're not doing it now. That is unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, Ms. Ruskovska, if anyone would claim the opposite before this Court, that all of you -- all of your colleagues and you yourself acted differently from what you stated now, this statement would simply be incorrect. It would not be the truth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed the cross-examination of this witness. I would like to ask the Court to receive into evidence the exhibits shown to this witness, 1D-180. That is under tab 1 in this binder. These are the excerpts from the Law on Criminal Procedure. Then 1D-181, which is under the tab 2 in the Court binder -- no, the first one -- I apologise. The first one is the Law on Public prosecutor's office. I apologise. Under tab 2 are the excerpts from the Law on Criminal Procedure, and our number is 1D-181. Then the document under tab 36 in your binder, which is 1D-177 as its number. Then tab 38, the document, our number 1D-178. And tab 39, our number 1D-179.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you wish to tender the documents at those five tabs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand from my discussions with my learned colleagues that there has been a problem with accessing certain English translations on e-court. However, it seems to me that the Code of Criminal Procedure has already been admitted as an exhibit, as has the Law of the Public Prosecutor, and perhaps even some more of the exhibits that Ms. Residovic recently referred to. And I'm concerned that by admitting now excerpts of the same exhibits that have already been admitted that we're simply going to confuse the record. That is my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe you're correct about those two laws. And is it right that the other three, tabs 36, 38, and 39, are each in the situation that in one language they're already an exhibit, but there is not a translation of an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regarding each of the documents, I indicated why is it we are tendering it as our evidence. First, the document on public prosecutor's office that the Prosecutor has in the e-court and which has been received as Prosecutor's Exhibit is not the document that we are offering; namely, the document that we are offering is the Law on Public Prosecutor's Office that was in use in 2002 -- 2001, while the exhibit that the Prosecutor tendered is the Law on Public Prosecutor's Office of a later date. With regards to the other exhibits that we indicated, there are numerous documents under one number. Those that we sought to tender, 36, 38, and 39, as you have stated already, they are part of P49, but they were not translated and we could not use them in the procedure. And number 2, it is true that we have the translation of the entire Law on Criminal Procedure, but it is not in the e-court and we think that only the relevant provisions which are important from the viewpoint of Defence, it is those that we seek to tender. 36, 38, and 39 are not translated at all, and we don't know how could we tender them without translation so that they could be shown to the witness during the cross-examination. We will follow your instructions, but this appeared to us as an attempt to clarify our situation and not to complicate it any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document at tab 1 will be received. It is the law in force in 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 1D11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As far as we understand, the other four documents are affected by the translation problem and the availability. I am informed by the court registry officer that if the translation is provided, that translation can be incorporated into the existing exhibit and then we will have what you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we didn't find these translations, we made translations that were given to you. I don't know whether the Prosecutor would ask translations for their exhibits, because so far they haven't been given to us. We have indicated even before that around half of the exhibits in the large files have not been translated, so we could ask that the Prosecutor ask the translation for these documents so then they are incorporated in the existing exhibits of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Play I try to clarify the matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will try and clarify things and not confuse them more. With respect, at least, to the Macedonian Law on Criminal Procedure, an English, a full English translation has been available for many months, if not years, and it is only because apparently of a technical mistake that this English translation has not yet been uploaded on to e-court. Simply, it was apparently placed in the right computer folder where the e-court technicians were supposed to have done it. Apparently, a mistake occurred and it is not available at this moment on e-court, but the Prosecution believes it can be a mistake that can be rectified very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We absolutely accept this proposal of my colleague. In respect to document number 2, we have no -- no problem putting in the e-court because it will probably be used on other occasion as well. But for the documents under the numbers 36, 38, 39, the Prosecutor never requested to be translated and these translation do not even exist. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct and I was going to address that, but I hadn't finished what I was going to say. Your Honours, tomorrow afternoon there will be a discussion in the interests of harmony between Defence counsel and members of the Prosecution team, in part about this very issue. There were documents within these voluminous court files which the Prosecution did not request to be translated into English. I don't believe it is half of them, but there were a number of documents which the Prosecution did not request to be translated into English because, quite frankly, the Prosecution when it reviewed all the document did not believe at that time that they would be relevant and so did not require translation. But we will review the entire list of these documents with members of the Defence tomorrow, and I believe we will be able to find a resolution for this. We can certainly request additional translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I suggest, Ms. Residovic, that documents at tabs 36, 38, and 39 simply be left aside for the moment to see whether there can be a resolution of the translation problem. If that can't be resolved, we will revive your motion and deal with it the way you propose. But if they can be incorporated into an existing exhibit, the translations, it would, I think, in the long run be more convenient for everybody. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, I take it, Mr. Apostolski remains, as he indicated, not wishing to cross-examine. So, Mr. Saxon

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, what does the term "effective control" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, my colleague asked you a question. It's at page 20 of today's transcript, and she asked you whether members -- whether the Minister of the Interior, in 2001, had effective control over members of the Ministry of Interior who were conducting investigations. So what does this concept of "effective control" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: The police is not carrying out investigation at all. The police participates in the pretrial procedure, so the investigation is carried out by the investigating judge and the request of the prosecutor. I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, when my colleague asked you whether the Minister of the Interior lacked effective control over persons in the Ministry of Interior who were investigating crimes, your response was positive. I don't recall your compacts words, but it was an affirmative response. I just need to explore with you what your understanding of this concept of effective control is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the transcript suggests the language used may have been whether there was any "effective role" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- rather than "control."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise then. Perhaps there has been a change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a question in which both the words "effective role" and "effective control" are used. So carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can, are you able to describe the meaning of this concept called "effective control"?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Could you please remind me of the entire conversation? I can't really remember what you're referring to. I would like to give a precise and accurate answer, but if you could about back to the transcript and please read to me what was said and make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What you said was something close to this: "Isn't it true that in 2001, the Minister of the Interior lacked effective control," i.e., he did not have effective control over persons in the Ministry of Interior who investigated crimes, and you responded in the affirmative?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, because basically the police stations on the level of the city of Skopje are carrying out investigations on any crimes that is committed, and they file the criminal reports. I do not believe that not this but at any other police minister has the control that is could know exactly what is going on and what criminal reports are filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So does that mean, in your mind, this concept "effective control" refers to whether, for example, a minister or another person in charge would know exactly what was going on below him?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Look. Probably the minister receives daily reports, or reports about the previous day, about the bigger things that has happened. And it is known who carries out the pre-trial procedure in the detection of the perpetrators and who prosecutes them. So listen, I don't know exactly. I don't know precisely. This is just an assumption that he is informed about the larger things that had happened in the country, and that the entire work is conducted by the competent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another point now. You explained to Ms. Residovic how, in 2001, the police performed their legal duty by informing an investigating judge and the public prosecutor when a crime may have occurred. And I wanted to ask you, well, what happened in 2001 if the police committed a crime? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Are you referring to a general criminal act or a criminal act conflicted to the conflict, because the police officers are also human. They can steal something sometimes. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know. I know. Let's speak in general terms. What would have happened in 2001 with respect to this legal duty to inform an investigating judge, to inform the public prosecutor. Well, suppose a police officer commits a crime. If that police officer's fellow colleagues --

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Then he would be reported as any other citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Suppose that --

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Basically, he would supposed to be reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Suppose that this hypothetical delinquent police officer committed a crime but his fellow officers did not report this event. Would it be fair then to say that these police officer colleagues weren't fulfilling their legal duty to inform the investigating judge or the public prosecutor? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes. By not informing the investigating judge, if a police officer commits a crime, a criminal report is filed and is sent to the public prosecutor. And I'm sure that if there is a check-up made in the public prosecutor's office in 2001, that there are certainly indicted police officers for crimes that have been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: As it happens always.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sure. My colleague read to you some portions of a statement that was provided by one of your colleagues, Mr. Serafimovski, to the Office of the Prosecutor, and one of the paragraphs that my colleague read to you said the following. Mr. Serafimovski heard that Atulla Qaili was hurt during the conflict with security forces in Ljuboten village, and then Mr. Serafimovski continued: "I learned from the press that the police were there," i.e., in the village of Ljuboten. Can you tell us what you learned during your investigation about the presence of police units or police officers in Ljuboten on the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. One last question, which I hope I can formulate simply. You've been shown a number of documents about proposals from Minister of the Interior and prosecutors about conducting -- possibly conducting an exhumation in the village of Ljuboten subsequent to the events of the 12th of August. And you also described how it was difficult to identify the perpetrators unless persons participating in the conflict named them. It was tough to identify who precisely had done what? And you also explained, I know very sincerely, that you and your colleagues tried to do your best but that there was a large amount of pressure on you at the time. I'd like to ask your opinion. At that time, August, September 2001, what would have been an easier method to establish the facts the about what happened in Ljuboten: Would it have been easier to plan and perform a exhumation in the village still in this conflicted area, or would it have been easier to speak to police officers who had been present in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Look. Where an investigation is carried out, as a prosecutor, you know it best, that the statements of the police officials are insufficient, so exhumation is necessary in order to see whether the statements are correct or not. So if one wants to have an impartial investigation, then both sides need to be interviewed and heard and to see the evidence. So the expert would be able to gather with us to attempt and to acquire a realistic picture about what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Ruskovska, in respect of the matter that has just been discussed with you by Mr. Saxon, if you have that bundle of papers, the folder of papers with you - it's just coming back to you now - if you'd turn to tab 28. It's quite a big bundle, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You indicated to Mr. Saxon that you knew nothing at the time about the conduct of the police at Ljuboten, particularly on the 10th to the 12th of August, I think, was the question. I wondered whether you would have been aware of this report that appeared to have been forwarded from Cair to the Basic Court at Skopje on the 3rd of September. The covering letter is that at tab 28, and the report itself is at tab 29. As I've understood your evidence, you had access to the material that was available to the investigating judge. Perhaps when you've familiarised yourself with these documents, you may be able to tell us whether you will access to this report at that time.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Since quite some time has passed, whether I have read this information or not, whether it was in my case or not, I can't really tell. But I think that this information and the point of my answer to the -- to Mr. Prosecutor was that even if he would have heard the police officers, and this is a police report, you can't really get the realistic picture about the events there. We then would only be able to see one side of the events. As a prosecutor, I can't be sure what has exactly happened if only one side is heard. And at that time, we were unable to enter Ljuboten - when I say "we," I refer to my colleagues, prosecutors, and investigating judges - in order to have a full on-site inspection, to get the full picture. I don't say that this information is incorrect. But whether it presents the realistic picture, I don't know, without conducting all the other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I could also ask you about tab 9. Were you aware at the time of the report of the 14th of August, which is at tab 9, from the sector for criminal techniques of the criminal police on the scientific testing for gun powder residue in respect of the persons that are named in that report, many of whom have been witnesses before us?

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: So what's your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you aware of this at the time? I know it's hard to remember back five years or so.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: Well, most probably. Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This report appears to be on the court file. I take it, it would, in the ordinary course, have been placed before the investigating judges on each of the relevant investigations.

utterances.speaker: VILMA RUSKOVSKA
utterances.text: I believe it was part of the court case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Court case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber, Mr. Saxon, has mentioned there three of the tabs which we hope will be the subject of your -- included in your discussions with other counsel about the translation process and the incorporation into the existing exhibit, because at the moment, well, I don't believe any one of those three is available other than here in an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We will certainly do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Ruskovska, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes your questioning in this case. It must be a novel experience to become a witness. I hope you will be able to look back on in the future with some --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give, and, of course, you may now leave and return to your home and work. Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, will the Chamber permit the Prosecution to use the remaining time by starting with its next witness or would the Chamber prefer that we defer this until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber understands there are two or three procedural matters to be raised before the next witness commences. If we can conclude any of those in the six minutes, we will; otherwise, we will deal with them first thing tomorrow morning before the next witness is called. We've now got only five minutes. I think I see Mr. Mettraux itching to get to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely. Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good evening. I think within the next five minutes, I will be able to deal with one of those issues, and that relates to the proposed consolidated statement of Mr. Henry Bolton, who is the next witness to appear. Your Honour will remember your order of the 25th, I believe, of April pursuant to Rule 92 ter concerning Mr. Bolton, and Your Honour's order was for the Prosecution to consolidate both of Mr. Bolton's statement, but not to include Mr. Bolton's investigator notes which he had begin to one of the Prosecution's investigator. We have identified a particular paragraph in the statement, the consolidate the statement of Mr. Bolton which would appear to come from his investigator's note and not from his statement. If I may direct Your Honour to paragraph 8 of that consolidate the statement. The problem is not so limited to the fact that a particular assertion was taken or lifted from the notes into the consolidated statement of Mr. Bolton. The main issue we have with this particular passage is it has been placed in the wrong place of Mr. Bolton's statement. If Your Honour has the benefit of the investigator's note, you will become aware that the content of this paragraph 8, in fact, relates to the 10th of August, 2001; whereas, in the consolidated statement, this particular assertion has been placed in the context of Mr. Bolton's visit or attempted visit on the 12th, which could be relatively misleading. We have no doubt it is an accident in the process of consolidating the statement; but we are just indicated that before Mr. Bolton come to give there evidence, it would seem possible perhaps that this paragraph be taken out as a whole or edited out so that this statement can be otherwise admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, are you in a position to comment on that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you will allow me, because I know time is limited, to go out on a limb, on a legal limb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will get our sores ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know. It is my best recollection that this particular information that is in paragraph 8 actually does refer to the Sunday, 12 of August, and it is my best recollection that while similar information may have been available in an investigator note, it's my best recollection that this information was also reflected in one of Mr. Bolton's actual signed statements. I will certainly go back and check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could we suggest, Mr. Saxon, that you look at the matter overnight, discuss it with Mr. Mettraux. If you find that it is properly in its present place, and if not, well, then, we may have to delete it from this written statement. Whether it would become the subject of oral question or not would be a matter consequential on that. I think we will leave it on that basis, that has used four of the five minutes. I think we will call it finished for the day there. Counsel may not have caught up with the fact that that tomorrow we have been moved from the afternoon to the morning, and we start at 9.00 in the morning in courtroom number II. We now adjourn for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
